title: The fever and the self
hookLine: a fever, two blankets, and a sage who answers it with a question
carry: i am the self, not only the body
tomorrow: how do you describe something only by saying what it isn't?

cards: Two blankets, a mug of tea going cold, a phone face down because the screen hurts to look at. A fever shrinks the world to the size of the body: the heat, the ache, the clock that won't move.
In the Brihadaranyaka, a sage sitting with a king reaches for exactly that picture. Yajnavalkya doesn't tell King Janaka that fevers aren't real.
He asks a question about someone who burns along with the body, and he leaves it hanging in the air.

teach.b: Here's the question, in plain words. If a person knew the self, and could say, I am this, then wanting what, and for whose sake, would that person burn along with the body? I am this, in Sanskrit, is ayam asmi.
All week, ayam has pointed: this self, right here. Now the one being pointed at answers in the first person. Look at what the verse leaves alone.

teach.h: THE ACHE STAYS; THE QUESTION ASKS.
teach.b: It doesn't promise the ache will stop. It doesn't call pain a mistake. The fever stays a fever.
What it questions is the second burning, the one that joins in: wanting what, for whom? Then the next verse turns all the way outward.

Whoever has found this self and woken up to it, the self that has entered this tangled, hard place, the body, is the maker of everything. The world is theirs. In fact, the text says, they are the world itself.
So the scene ends somewhere unexpected. The self that looked trapped under two blankets is, in this verse, as wide as the world.

teach.h: ATMAN: THE SELF IN THE BODY.
teach.b: This is the Hindu teaching of atman: you are the self that lives in the body, not only the body it lives in.
It's why a grandmother can say through a fever, I am not this fever, and mean it as faith, not denial.

how: Students of the Brihadaranyaka read these verses within Yajnavalkya's teaching to King Janaka, where 'I am this' is set as a question about why one would suffer along with the body.

o: a pledge to care for one's body like a temple
this self is Brahman: 'I am this', so why burn?
a saying that the self is the body and nothing more

games.q: the verse and the one after it. tap the pairs.
p: the tangled place the self has entered
what the text says the knower is

s: the text says knowing the self makes the body stop aching
it leaves the ache alone and asks: wanting what, for whom, would one burn along with the body?
the great saying, in the first person.
the next verse says the one who wakes to this self is the world itself
the maker of everything; the world is theirs.

games.q: your friend sprains her ankle the week of the big game and spends every night spiraling about it. what fits the verse?
o: tell her to pretend it doesn't hurt; the verse says pain isn't real.
nothing to do until it heals; the body decides everything.
the ankle hurts; gently ask what the second burning, the spiral, is for.
games.why: the verse never denies the ache. it asks about the burning that joins in: wanting what, for whose sake?

practice: Sit as you are and rest one hand on a place that's tight or tired: the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach. Let the ache be exactly what it is, and breathe under your hand.
Then rest in the one who is noticing, and let the verse's question sit there with you: wanting what, for whom?

wordCard.voice: Ayam atma brahma, this self is Brahman, said in the first person: ayam asmi, I am this. Knowing it, the text asks, why burn along with the body?

orig.note: Sanskrit: ayam asmi, I am this, in Brihadaranyaka 4.4.12.

carryVoice: To carry: i am the self, not only the body. The ache is real; the self doesn't have to burn along with it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.12 (if a person knew the self, 'I am this', wishing what, for whose desire, would he burn along with the body?)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.13 (whoever has found and awakened to the self that has entered this tangled, perilous place is the maker of all; the world is his; he is the world itself)
